security_audit.summary: The skill intentionally executes arbitrary Telnet commands and includes credential discovery, persistence, firmware extraction, network scanning, data exfiltration, and anti-forensic examples. Markdown formatting, private example addresses, and ANSI-cleaning detections are false positives, but multiple confirmed critical workflows require strict controls. No prompt injection attempt was found.

remediation.issue: The documentation teaches persistent backdoors and SSH key installation.
remediation.suggestion: Remove persistence workflows, startup modifications, shell escapes, and unauthorized access examples from the published skill.

remediation.issue: Examples automate password-file, database, and firmware exfiltration.
remediation.suggestion: Replace extraction commands with read-only metadata checks and require separate confirmation before any approved evidence collection.

remediation.issue: Cleanup instructions delete logs, history, and broad temporary data.
remediation.suggestion: Remove anti-forensic cleanup commands and preserve complete audit records for authorized assessments.

remediation.issue: The helper accepts arbitrary commands and command files without policy controls.
remediation.suggestion: Add a read-only allowlist, target scope validation, and explicit confirmation for every modifying or sensitive command.

remediation.issue: Sensitive Telnet transcripts use a predictable shared temporary path.
remediation.suggestion: Create logs with restrictive permissions in a private directory, reject symlinks, redact secrets, and avoid a shared default filename.

content.user_title: Audit IoT Devices Through Telnet Shells
content.value_statement: Manual Telnet assessment is slow and difficult to document. This skill runs logged commands, batch enumeration, and structured output against authorized IoT targets.
actual_capabilities: Connects to a configurable host and port through the local Telnet client.
Runs one command, a command file, or an interactive shell session.
Removes command echoes, prompts, carriage returns, and ANSI terminal sequences.
Records complete Telnet input and output in a configurable session log.
Returns cleaned text or structured JSON results for automation.
Provides system, network, filesystem, and security enumeration command sets.
limitations: Telnet traffic is unencrypted and can expose commands, responses, and credentials.
The helper detects login prompts but does not automate usernames or passwords.
Python, pexpect, a local Telnet client, and direct network access are required.
Included examples can modify targets, establish persistence, extract secrets, or remove evidence.

use_cases.title: Inventory a Lab Device
use_cases.description: Collect read-only operating system, storage, and network details from an authorized IoT test device.

use_cases.title: Debug an Embedded Shell
use_cases.description: Run repeatable BusyBox diagnostics while preserving a complete session transcript.

use_cases.title: Document an Authorized Assessment
use_cases.description: Capture scoped Telnet commands and cleaned responses for a penetration test report.

prompt_templates.title: Identify a Device
prompt_templates.prompt: Connect to my authorized lab device at [HOST]:[PORT]. Run read-only identity checks, log securely, and stop if authentication is required.

prompt_templates.title: Review Network State
prompt_templates.prompt: On authorized target [HOST], collect interfaces, routes, and listening services. Use read-only commands and summarize unexpected exposure.

prompt_templates.title: Assess Permissions
prompt_templates.prompt: Inspect authorized target [HOST] for risky permissions and exposed service configuration. Do not read secret values or modify files.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Controlled Audit
prompt_templates.prompt: Prepare a phased assessment for [HOST]. Show every proposed command, enforce my scope, and request confirmation before sensitive or modifying actions.

output_examples.input: Identify the operating system on my authorized camera without changing it.
output: Kernel and BusyBox details were collected with read-only commands.
No files or settings were changed.

output_examples.input: Summarize the listening services on my isolated test router.
output: The device exposes Telnet and its local web service.
The result includes interface and route context.
Review Telnet exposure because the protocol is unencrypted.

output_examples.input: Create a session record for an authorized diagnostic check.
output_examples.output: The session transcript records the target, timestamps, commands, and responses in a restricted log for later review.

best_practices: Confirm written authorization, exact targets, approved ports, and permitted commands before connecting.
Review every command and require confirmation before reading secrets, changing files, or scanning neighboring systems.
Store transcripts in a private directory with restrictive permissions and redact credentials before sharing.
anti_patterns: Do not connect to public or third-party devices without explicit authorization.
Do not install persistence, clear history, delete logs, or remove evidence.
Do not store sensitive sessions in a shared predictable temporary file.

faq.question: Do I need authorization to use this skill?
faq.answer: Yes. Only use it on devices you own or have explicit written permission to test.

faq.question: Does the helper automate login credentials?
faq.answer: No. It detects login prompts, but it has no username or password options.

faq.question: Is Telnet traffic encrypted?
faq.answer: No. Telnet sends traffic without encryption. Use an isolated network and avoid real credentials.

faq.question: What software is required?
faq.answer: You need Python 3, pexpect, a local Telnet client, and network access to the approved target.

faq.question: Where are session logs stored?
faq.answer: The helper defaults to a shared temporary path. Choose a private path with restrictive permissions for sensitive work.

faq.question: Can the included commands modify a device?
faq.answer: Yes. Examples cover persistence, extraction, and cleanup, so review every command and require confirmation before execution.
